high_priority_articles.title: Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) Latest News - Vajiram & Ravi
high_priority_articles.summary: Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) Latest News  Vajiram & Ravi
high_priority_articles.full_text:
- The United States Trade Representative (USTR) has launched an investigation into the European Union’s expansion of its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) — a move that could escalate trade tensions between the two blocs.
- The USTR has invited public comments from American small businesses till November 9. Seeking public comments is typically the first step toward possible retaliation — signalling the US may push the EU to soften CBAM’s implementation.
- For India, this development carries an unusual silver lining: any US-driven softening of CBAM could automatically benefit Indian exporters too, thanks to a clause in the India-EU trade deal.
What Is CBAM, and Why Is the US Investigating It?
- CBAM is the EU’s carbon pricing mechanism. It requires EU importers of goods in six carbon-intensive sectors to declare the embedded emissions of imported products and pay a carbon price equivalent to what EU domestic producers already pay.
- Covered Sectors: Aluminium; Cement; Electricity; Fertiliser; Hydrogen; Iron and steel.
The US’s Specific Complaint
- The EU calculates default emission values using country- and sector-level production/energy data.
- However, the EU adds a punitive mark-up to these default values — a measure meant to push companies toward submitting verified company-level data instead.
- Any company-level data must be verified by an EU-accredited third-party verifier — adding cost and compliance burden, which the US says disproportionately hurts American small businesses.
How India Stands to Benefit
- India had tough negotiations with the EU over CBAM while finalising the India-EU trade deal, since the regulation is expected to hit a wide range of Indian metal exports.
- Crucially, however, Indian negotiators secured a ‘forward-Most Favoured Nation’ (MFN) CBAM clause.
- What this clause does – It ensures that any concession the EU grants to another trading partner (here, the US) under a separate agreement automatically extends to India too.
  - In the EU-US trade deal joint statement (August last year), the EU had already committed: “…the European Commission… commits to work to provide additional flexibilities in the CBAM implementation” for US businesses.
  - If the ongoing USTR probe results in further CBAM flexibilities for the US, India would also receive those same concessions — without needing to renegotiate separately.
The Stakes for Indian Industry
- According to the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), CBAM could translate into a 20–35% tax on select Indian exports — particularly iron, steel, and aluminium — into the EU.
- This is effectively being called a steel bill for India.
- Added complication — Steel Scrap
  - The EU is the world’s largest producer of steel scrap, and its move to curb steel-scrap exports, combined with CBAM, acts as a non-tariff barrier against Indian industry.
  - Despite Indian objections, the EU kept CBAM outside the scope of the India-EU trade deal.
- Why Production Method Matters
  - Blast furnace–basic oxygen furnace (BF-BOF) route: highest emissions.
  - Gas-based direct reduced iron (DRI): lower emissions.
  - Scrap-based electric arc furnace (EAF) route: lowest emissions.
- India’s Vulnerability: Indian manufacturers largely rely on the blast furnace route, making them currently underprepared for CBAM’s carbon-price burden.
India’s Response: The Green Steel Push
- The government plans to scale up scrap-based steel production via electric arc furnace technology, under its Green Steel Initiative.
- However, a May 2025 report by the Indian Council for Research on International Economic Relations (ICRIER) flagged a major constraint:
  - Scrap currently makes up only 20% of India’s steelmaking feedstock.
  - This is limited by domestic scrap availability of just ~25 Million Metric Tonnes (MMt) annually.
  - The report notes: hard-to-abate sectors like steel face unprecedented pressure to decarbonise amid tools like CBAM, with scrap steel central to this transition — yet India’s constrained scrap access remains a critical bottleneck.
Conclusion
- The US probe into CBAM is, at its core, a dispute over how the EU prices carbon at its borders — but it has inadvertently opened a door for India.
- Thanks to a carefully negotiated MFN clause, any flexibility the EU grants the US could flow to Indian exporters too, without further bargaining.
- Yet this remains a short-term cushion, not a solution: India’s long-term competitiveness in a carbon-taxed world will depend on how fast it can scale scrap-based, low-emission steel production — a transition still constrained by domestic scrap scarcity.
Source: IE

high_priority_articles.title: Fed minutes: Another rate hike likely coming this year to combat persistent inflation - ABC7 Chicago
high_priority_articles.summary: Fed minutes: Another rate hike likely coming this year to combat persistent inflation  ABC7 Chicago
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Federal Reserve officials are expecting another interest rate increase in 2026.
WASHINGTON, D.C. -- Most Federal Reserve officials expect that another interest rate increase will likely be needed this year to combat inflation, according to minutes released Wednesday from the central bank’s most recent meeting.
The officials unanimously agreed that inflation was still elevated and had not made much progress toward their 2% target in recent months, the minutes said. The Fed increased its key interest rate at the Sept. 15-16 meeting by a quarter-point to about 3.9%, its first increase in three years.
The increase defied President Donald Trump’s repeated calls for the Fed to cut rates and prompted the president to criticize the Fed’s rate-setting committee, though he still expressed support for Chairman Kevin Warsh, whom he appointed earlier this year. The rate increase comes as Americans are already struggling with high costs for groceries, gas, and housing, and as affordability has taken on a leading role in the upcoming midterm elections, just seven weeks away.
Longer-term interest rates for mortgages and other borrowing have also jumped in the past few months for a range of reasons, including rising government debt, heavy borrowing by tech firms to finance data center construction, climbing oil and gas prices, and signs that growth and inflation remain elevated. The Fed’s rate hike has likely played only a limited role in the increase.
Still, key policymakers have said since the meeting that the Fed can take some time to monitor the economy and the impact of last month’s rate hike before making another move. Wall Street investors now forecast the Fed will keep its rate unchanged at its next meeting Oct. 28-29, according to futures pricing, and raise it when they meet in December.
Philip Jefferson, vice chair of the Fed’s board of governors, said last week that policymakers “will need to come to our own judgment, which may take more time.”
Inflation, according to the Fed’s preferred measure, came in lower than many economists expected in August but remained elevated. Overall prices rose 3.4% compared with a year earlier, while core prices — which exclude volatile food and energy categories — increased 3%. On a monthly basis, prices rose 0.3% from July to August, and core prices just 0.2%.
According to the minutes, even with the rise in longer-term rates, many officials said that financial conditions—which includes rising stock prices — “appeared to be supportive of economic growth,” a sign that more rate hikes may be needed to cool the economy.
Several policymakers said that they saw the Fed’s rate as too low to restrain the economy, or only acting as a mild restraint. That suggests they would support multiple rate hikes to rein in inflation.
Higher oil and gas prices stemming from the Iran war and the lingering effects of tariffs have lifted costs in recent months. But even excluding those trends, many Fed officials believe inflation is stuck between 2.5% and 3%, above its target. Spiking prices for semiconductors, computer equipment, and electrical components due to the rapid surge in data center construction have also played a big role in accelerating inflation.
The Fed lifted its key interest rate to about 3.9% at its Sept. 15-16 meeting, its first increase in three years. Higher rates are intended to slow borrowing and spending, cool the economy, and bring down inflation.
Warsh emphasized after the announcement that the economy has shown signs of gathering speed since the central bank decided to keep rates unchanged in late July.
“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Warsh said at a news conference after last month’s meeting. “We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective clearly and at sufficient speed. Today the FOMC decided that this standard has not been satisfied,” he added, referring to the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee, an arm of the Fed.
Trump criticized the committee for voting to raise rates, calling them “very political,” but he did not single out Warsh.
“They’re raising rates to make Trump do as bad as they can possibly do,” the president said.

high_priority_articles.title: JPMorgan's David Kelly Expects Fed To Keep Interest Rates Unchanged After In-Line CPI Report — 'We Essentially Have Got Teflon Inflation In America' - Stocktwits
high_priority_articles.summary: JPMorgan's David Kelly Expects Fed To Keep Interest Rates Unchanged After In-Line CPI Report — 'We Essentially Have Got Teflon Inflation In America'  Stocktwits
high_priority_articles.full_text:
JPMorgan Asset Management’s Chief Global Strategist, David Kelly, expects the Federal Reserve to leave interest rates unchanged, saying the latest CPI report reinforces a gradual disinflationary trend despite persistent price pressures.
During an interview with Bloomberg, Kelly said policymakers should let inflation cool on its own rather than trying to accelerate the process, arguing that wage growth remains too weak to sustain persistent price pressures.
Kelly pointed to lower tariff costs and an eventual decline in oil prices as factors that could ease inflation. However, he believes that the rate of wage growth is the more apparent reason he does not expect inflation to become entrenched, noting that wages have risen less than CPI inflation for four consecutive months.
“American workers can't get a raise. And if they can't, you cannot have sticky inflation,” he said.
Kelly said inflation has remained elevated after a series of supply shocks and policy decisions, including the COVID-19 response, the war in Ukraine, tariffs and the Iran war. He said inflation should gradually come down if policymakers back away from some of those pressures.
“We essentially have got Teflon inflation in America… it won’t stick. You could do no good by trying to hurry this process. It’s like an injury. It just heals slowly… if you try and speed it up you’re just going to mess everything up,” he added.
Kelly criticized what he described as the Fed’s move toward communicating less, saying the central bank has a “real communications problem.” Kelly said Fed Chair Kevin Warsh should reflect the consensus within the committee and clearly communicate its thinking to markets.
“He is going to have to back off a little bit from his very aggressive rhetoric and say and admit and acknowledge there’s some progress in inflation,” said Kelly, while adding that Warsh’s upcoming Jackson Hole speech later this month will be important.
U.S. consumer prices inched up in July and were in line with expectations, according to the Consumer Price Index (CPI) report released earlier on Wednesday.
Data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) showed that CPI rose 0.1% in July on a seasonally adjusted basis, with the annual inflation rate cooling to 3.4% from 3.5% last month.
Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.2% in July, in line with expectations, according to MarketWatch data.
The in-line CPI print also resulted in a fall in rate hike odds. According to data from the CME FedWatch tool, the odds of a 25 basis point rate hike in September fell to 37.9% on Wednesday, from 48.4% a day ago and 54.4% a week ago.
At the time of writing, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), which tracks the S&P 500 index, gained 0.29%; the Invesco QQQ Trust ETF (QQQ) rose 0.85%; and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) edged up by 0.09%. Retail sentiment on Stocktwits regarding the S&P 500 ETF was in the ‘neutral’ territory.
The iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT) was up 0.11%, while the iShares 7-10 Year Treasury Bond ETF (IEF) gained 0.19%.

high_priority_articles.title: Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’ - The Guardian
high_priority_articles.summary: Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’  The Guardian
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Donald Trump has announced an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, apparently without consulting Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said the deal to stop long-range attacks was “news to me”.
In a social media post, the US president claimed the two sides had reached an agreement. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social.
He offered no further details. Zelenskyy said he was surprised by the announcement but would agree to it if Vladimir Putin did the same. “If President Trump negotiated it with Putin – please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready and we will accept it,” the Ukrainian president told the Axios website.
Earlier, Zelenskyy rebuffed Trump’s demand made on Saturday that Kyiv stop bombing Russian oil refineries. Zelenskyy said Moscow had to first halt its own “brutal” attacks on his country’s energy infrastructure.
Any deal to end long-range drone strikes by Ukraine on targets inside Russia would have to be “reciprocal”, he said. It should be backed by “real guarantees” – meaning punitive measures against Moscow from Ukraine’s allies, including the US.
There was no sign that the Kremlin was observing Trump’s ceasefire. According to Zelenskyy, Russian drones took to the sky “throughout the day” on Sunday. There were also “unfortunately” several airstrikes, he said, including on energy infrastructure.
The Ukrainian president said the Russians hit thermal power station No 5 in the eastern city of Kharkiv – the latest of more than 200 strikes this week against electricity generation and transmission facilities in Ukraine. There were another 17 hits on gas and oil facilities, he added.
The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.
A furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump said Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader”, he said on Saturday.
Responding to Trump, Zelenskyy said it was up to Ukrainians to choose “one or another leader”. He told ABC News he was willing to accept Trump’s demands and to organise elections, but only if Putin agreed to a “total” 60-day ceasefire.
The bitter public feud is the most serious between the US and Ukraine since last year, when Trump berated Zelenskyy in the Oval Office.
The Financial Times, citing officials in Europe, reported on Sunday that the US is threatening to stop the procurement system that provides Ukraine with weapons to press Kyiv to halt its deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
The New York Times has reported that US officials have offered the Kremlin lucrative economic incentives in exchange for a ceasefire. They reportedly include releasing billions in Russian sovereign assets that are frozen. The Trump administration also revisited a plan to sell parts of Russia’s energy company, Lukoil. The multibillion deal would benefit Middle Eastern investors, the paper reported, some with “business ties” to US negotiators.
On Saturday, Trump criticised Zelenskyy and said he had refused to make a deal to end the fighting. In response, Ukraine’s president laid the blame for Europe’s biggest war since 1945 on “Russia and Russia alone”. “It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so,” he said.
Ukrainian officials point out that the White House is demanding Kyiv give up its most effective weapon, without demanding any corresponding concessions from Russia. In recent weeks, Kyiv has dealt a major blow to Russia’s economy, striking oil complexes, warehouses and datacentres.
Russia’s own bombing campaign has been relentless. On Saturday it killed 23 people in the city of Zaporizhzhia, including four children, and hit a five-storey apartment block in the frontline town of Sloviansk. Zelenskyy said Moscow’s aerial campaign involved thousands of aerial bombs and jet-powered drones. It continued “unabated”, he said.
The head of Ukraine’s foreign affairs committee, Oleksandr Merezhko, said Trump’s “bullying” demand for Zelenskyy to quit had strengthened him at home “paradoxically”, after recent damaging corruption scandals. “Putin’s plan is to decapitate Zelenskyy and remove him as a wartime leader. Trump is siding with Putin,” Merezhko said.
He added: “I’m afraid that behind this situation is Trump’s worldview. He wants to do business with Putin. For him, Ukraine seems like an obstacle to be removed. Both Trump and Putin wish to pressure us into capitulation.”
Referring to the notorious 1939 agreement between Nazi Germany and the USSR, Merezhko said: “We are moving to a new Molotov-Ribbentrop pact and to a world of strongmen and spheres of influence.”
Merezhko said Ukraine would continue to destroy enemy oil refineries, against US wishes, because they funded Russia’s war machine and acknowledged that a cutoff of US intelligence sharing with Kyiv – threatened by the Trump administration – would “blind” Ukraine’s air defence systems. “This would be an act of complicity with Putin’s genocide. It would mean more dead civilians and dead children,” he said.
Ukrainian negotiators had been meeting in Florida with their American counterparts, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, when Trump announced the US was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel. Blindsided, the Ukrainians went home early. “It felt like a trap,” one stunned Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent newspaper.
On Sunday, Zelenskyy shored up support in a series of conversations with key allies including Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, the Polish leader, Donald Tusk, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen.
Earlier Zelenskyy spoke with the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb. Downing Street said Burnham recognised the last 24 hours had been “difficult” for Ukraine and “reiterated his complete solidarity”.
Downing Street said the two leaders agreed “to maintain pressure on Russia” and to strengthen the sanctions regime, despite Trump’s efforts to the contrary. “Russia should agree to an immediate energy ceasefire, ending its brutal strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure and its attacks on shipping in the Black Sea,” a statement added.
Speaking over the weekend, Zelenskyy said Trump’s decision empowered Putin and gave him “extra money for the war”, running into millions and “perhaps billions”. “It is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should act. And, in my view, it is a weak decision,” he said.
- Luke Harding’s Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest is published by Guardian Faber

high_priority_articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Russia attacks multiple power plants after Trump energy ceasefire claim - The Guardian
high_priority_articles.summary: Ukraine war briefing: Russia attacks multiple power plants after Trump energy ceasefire claim  The GuardianTrump says Ukraine and Russia have agreed 'energy ceasefire'  BBCPutin has already broken Trump's 'energy ceasefire' with attack on power plant, says Zelenskyy  Sky NewsTrump claims Ukraine and Russia have agreed to energy ceasefire | CNN Politics  CNNTrump’s fantasy ceasefire tricks no one  The Telegraph
high_priority_articles.full_text:
- Russian strikes hit multiple Ukrainian power plants after Donald Trump claimed both sides had agreed to stop hitting each other’s energy infrastructure, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. The Ukrainian president said on social media a drone had hit a power plant in Kyiv on Sunday, leading to power outages in the capital. Shortly after, he said there had been a strike on the CHP-5 power plant in the eastern city of Kharkiv, adding:“Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian ‘shaheds’ [drones] all day.”
- Trump said earlier that “effective immediately, there is an energy ceasefire in the war between Russia and Ukraine”. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” the US president wrote on his Truth Social platform on Sunday morning in Washington, without further details. Zelenskyy expressed surprise at the announcement, saying the deal was “news to me” and he was seeking further details. Russia has yet to confirm it agreed.
- The ceasefire appeared to garner support on Sunday from Ukraine’s key western allies, including the UK, France, Canada and the European Commission. British prime minister Andy Burnham said a sustained energy ceasefire was “the best route to get energy and fuel back into world markets”. French president Emmanuel Macron said Paris supported a “real energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine.
- Ukrainian officials said Russian attacks killed six people in two Ukrainian cities on Sunday, including a strike on a grocery store in Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city, where three people died and 20 were injured. Two children were among the injured, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said. In a separate attack in western Ukraine, officials said a Russian strike killed three people.
- Trump’s energy truce claim came two days after he announced a controversial agreement to buy Russian diesel fuel while temporarily easing US sanctions, prompting outrage from Ukraine and its European allies, who said it would embolden Moscow. Canadian prime minister Mark Carney added to the chorus of disapproval after a Sunday call with Zelenskyy, saying the diesel deal “is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe”. EU chief Ursula von der Leyen also backed Zelenskyy “as he leads the fight for his people’s freedom”, while Germany foreign minister Johann Wadephul said Berlin continued to “fully support” him.
- Trump lashed out at Zelenskyy when asked about criticism of the Russia diesel deal, saying it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president” who would finally settle the war. Zelenskyy pushed back, telling US ABC News on Sunday: “First of all, with all respect to President Trump, it’s up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader.”
- The Trump administration is threatening to stop the procurement system that provides Ukraine with weapons in order to press Kyiv to halt its deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, the Financial Times quoted officials in Europe as saying. The US was lobbying European capitals and Kyiv in an attempt to end the attacks on Russian oil refineries, they said.
- A Ukrainian drone killed one person in Russia’s border Belgorod region on Sunday, officials said. The operational headquarters in Belgorod region said the drone struck a car on a road near the border. In the part of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region held by Russian forces, Moscow-installed officials said one person had been killed in a Ukrainian attack.
- Russia’s military said it struck a logistics centre in southern Ukraine’s Mykolaiv region and a cargo vessel in the Black Sea. The logistics centre in the town of Ternivka was used to store military and dual-use cargoes for the Ukrainian military, the Russian defence ministry claimed on Sunday.

high_priority_articles.title: NATO Is Winning the War Russia Isn’t Fighting - Modern Diplomacy
high_priority_articles.summary: NATO Is Winning the War Russia Isn’t Fighting  Modern Diplomacy
high_priority_articles.full_text:
On 23 September, a Russian Mi-8 helicopter flying from Kaliningrad crossed into Polish airspace north of the town of Braniewo, penetrated roughly 300 metres and stayed for 42 seconds before turning back. Polish fighter jets were scrambled, ground-based air defences went on standby, and Poland’s Operational Command concluded that Russia was once again testing the readiness of its air defences. By any measurable standard, it was a non-event. No shots were fired, nothing was damaged and nobody was hurt. That is exactly why it matters.
Twelve days later, the head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service told the Bundestag that Russia is waging a “shadow war” against Germany. Within days, the Atlantic Council published a report arguing that years of reinforcing NATO’s eastern flank have done little to discourage Russian sabotage, cyberattacks and drone incursions. The convergence is notable. European intelligence services, the EU’s defence commissioner and a leading Washington think tank are now describing the same problem in almost identical terms. NATO has become very good at deterring a war Russia is not currently trying to fight, and remains poorly equipped for the one it is fighting.
A conflict without a threshold
Hybrid warfare is not a new concept, and neither is the vocabulary used to describe it. What has changed is its texture. A US Helsinki Commission study grouped Russian operations inside NATO territory into four categories: attacks on critical infrastructure, violence campaigns, weaponised migration, and election interference and information operations. The Atlantic Council’s Agnia Grigas adds a more troubling observation: these operations increasingly carry a kinetic component and are persistent rather than episodic, forming a continuous pressure campaign rather than a series of isolated provocations.
Poland’s recent months illustrate the pattern. In July, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile entered Polish airspace and came down in a field in the east of the country. On 15 September, an unidentified drone approached the US ballistic missile defence base at Redzikowo. Two days later, Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned of a real risk that drones or missiles could fly into eastern-flank states and cause destruction. Then came the helicopter, which appears to be the first publicly reported case of a Russian military helicopter crossing Poland’s land border. In Germany, the intelligence chief Martin Jäger pointed to an attempted Russian drone attack on Leipzig airport on 31 July.
None of these incidents, taken individually, comes close to triggering Article 5. That is the design. Each is calibrated to sit beneath the threshold at which collective defence is invoked, while remaining visible enough to probe defences, signal intent and impose costs: scrambled jets, closed airspace, diverted resources and political anxiety. The cumulative effect is to normalise a higher baseline of risk. What would have been a crisis in 2021 is a routine Wednesday in 2026.
Moscow rejects this characterisation entirely. Its embassy has insisted that Russia poses no threat to NATO and has no intention of confronting it. Attribution in individual cases is sometimes contested, and analysts should resist folding every incident into a single narrative. But German, Danish and Polish authorities have assessed the pattern independently, and their conclusions are consistent enough that the burden of explanation has shifted.
Built for the wrong war
NATO’s conventional posture has been transformed since 2022. Defence budgets have risen, eastern-flank battlegroups have expanded, and Poland is building a network of bunkers, barriers, sensors and potential minefields along its borders with Belarus and Kaliningrad, with similar work under way in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. The Atlantic Council estimates that Russia maintains around 40,000 ground troops in the wider Baltic region, a figure it believes could be raised to roughly 100,000 by shifting forces from western Russia.
That investment is not wasted. A credible conventional defence is the reason a large-scale invasion remains unlikely, and Jäger himself said the BND sees no signs that Russia is preparing one. But this is where the asymmetry lies. Deterring conventional formations is now well resourced; countering persistent grey-zone pressure remains fragmented. The alliance’s decision-making is built around a binary, attack or no attack, with Article 5 as the hinge. Russia’s strategy is to operate permanently in the space between.
There is an uncomfortable irony here. The more credible NATO’s conventional deterrence becomes, the more rational it is for Moscow to shift pressure downward, into the domain where acting is cheapest and punishment is hardest. Success on one rung of the escalation ladder pushes the contest onto another.
The case for making Moscow pay, and why it is harder than it sounds
Grigas’s prescription is straightforward. Allies must persuade the Kremlin that hostile action carries predictable, material costs, using a pre-agreed menu of options: targeted sanctions, restrictions on Russian and Belarusian travel, trade and transit, large-scale diplomatic expulsions and cyber operations. Future drone incursions, attempted assassinations and sabotage, she argues, should prompt responses that are proportionate, coordinated and pre-agreed rather than mere condemnation. The EU’s defence commissioner, Andrius Kubilius, has said answers to hybrid attacks should be as painful as the attacks themselves. Kurt Volker, a former US ambassador to NATO, has asked openly where the line is that Russia would have to cross to provoke a response.
The argument has obvious appeal. Predictability is the core of deterrence, and Russia arguably exploits ambiguity in NATO’s responses more than ambiguity in its own actions. Yet the proposal runs into three problems that its advocates tend to understate.
The first is attribution. Hybrid operations are built for deniability, and Jäger has warned that Moscow may use false-flag operations designed to conceal the real perpetrator and complicate the response. An automatic response requires an agreed standard of proof, and 32 governments with different intelligence capacities and risk tolerances will not easily converge on one. A mechanism that fires on contested attribution hands Moscow a propaganda victory. One that waits for certainty is not automatic.
The second is consensus. The costs of retaliation fall unevenly. Restricting transit to Kaliningrad is borne disproportionately by Lithuania; measures against Belarus land hardest on Poland and Latvia. A menu agreed in Brussels must be executed in capitals with very different exposures, and some governments in both NATO and the EU have repeatedly shown reluctance to sign up to new measures against Russia.
The third is escalation. Part of the logic of the grey zone is that it allows both sides to avoid a war neither wants. A published schedule of penalties raises the cost of provocation, but it also hands initiative to whoever defines the triggers, and gives Moscow a map of exactly where to operate just beneath them. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte’s insistence that the alliance has response options that are not always public and not always tit for tat is often read as complacency. It can equally be read as a judgement that strategic ambiguity is itself a deterrent. That position deserves more serious engagement than its critics usually give it.
Germany moves to the front line
The most significant shift in this week’s debate is geographic. For years, “front line” in European security discourse meant the Baltic states, Poland and Romania. Jäger’s testimony relocated it. He said that no other country poses such a direct, comprehensive and concrete threat to Germany than Russia, which he argued is imposing the confrontation on Berlin because of its support for Ukraine and the Baltic states. He also warned that it would be a great illusion to assume the conflict with Russia will end when the war in Ukraine does.
That last point is the analytical core of the issue. If the shadow war is not a by-product of the war in Ukraine but a durable feature of Russian–European relations, then treating it as a crisis to be managed until a ceasefire is a category error. It becomes a permanent condition to be governed, through infrastructure resilience, investigative and prosecutorial capacity, intelligence sharing and the political willingness to name perpetrators publicly. European authorities are growing bolder in publicly identifying the states and organisations they hold responsible, which is a necessary first step.
It also raises an institutional question that the debate tends to skip: who owns this problem? Much of what Russia targets, including airports, rail networks, energy grids, undersea cables and elections, falls within national law enforcement and EU competences rather than NATO’s military remit. The alliance can deter armoured divisions; it cannot investigate a sabotage cell in Leipzig. The EU holds the regulatory, sanctions and legal tools, while NATO holds the military signalling. The deterrence gap persists partly because neither institution fully owns it.
What closing the gap would actually require
A credible response is less likely to come from a single new doctrine than from tightening the seams between existing ones. That means a shared attribution framework that allows faster, coordinated public attribution; sanctions packages drafted in advance and held in reserve, so that speed does not depend on fresh negotiation among 27 or 32 governments; infrastructure resilience treated as a core component of defence spending rather than an afterthought; and a clearer division of labour between NATO and the EU on hybrid threats.
None of this is as dramatic as “making Moscow pay”, and none of it will end the campaign. The realistic objective is not to stop hybrid operations altogether, which no deterrence postu

high_priority_articles.title: Russia lost more than 50,000 troops in a month, Ukraine 10 times fewer — NATO - Українські Національні Новини (УНН)
high_priority_articles.summary: Russia lost more than 50,000 troops in a month, Ukraine 10 times fewer — NATO  Українські Національні Новини (УНН)
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Kyiv • UNN
According to NATO's assessment, Russia lost more than 50,000 troops in September, while Ukraine lost around 5,000. The figures have not been independently verified.
In September 2026, the Russian army suffered more than 50,000 military personnel killed and wounded in Ukraine. Of these, up to 28,000 were killed. Bloomberg reports this, citing a senior NATO military official, writes UNN.
Details
According to the Alliance official's estimates, Ukrainian forces lost around 5,000 military personnel over the same period. Thus, according to these estimates, the Russian army's total losses were approximately 10 times higher.
The publication's source explained that the Russian command continues to send its units on the offensive through so-called kill zones, where troops come under strikes from drones and artillery and encounter minefields.
The war is becoming increasingly costly for Russia
According to Bloomberg, Ukrainian forces have also intensified strikes on facilities deep inside Russia, including oil refineries and data centers. At the same time, during ground operations, the Defense Forces regained control of more than 125 square kilometers of territory.
Against the backdrop of significant losses, the Russian authorities continue to increase military spending. In 2026, Russia's defense budget is expected to reach 17 trillion rubles, or approximately $199 billion. This is 40% more than the initial plan presented at the end of 2025.
At the same time, the Kremlin is not publishing official data on the losses suffered by its army or the scale of recruitment of new military personnel. It is currently impossible to independently verify NATO's estimates.

high_priority_articles.title: UK exports to Uzbekistan could exceed £1bn within a decade, says Lord Sarwar - Daryo
high_priority_articles.summary: UK exports to Uzbekistan could exceed £1bn within a decade, says Lord Sarwar  Daryo
high_priority_articles.full_text:
British Trade Minister identifies financial services, mining, clean energy and technology as key areas for deeper economic cooperation with Uzbekistan
UK exports to Uzbekistan could exceed £1bn within the next five to ten years, Trade Minister Lord Sarwar has told Daryo in an exclusive interview, outlining Britain’s ambitions to deepen commercial ties with Central Asia’s largest economy and expand cooperation in sectors ranging from financial services and mining to clean energy and digital technology.
UK exports to Uzbekistan increased from £66mn in 2016 to £592mn in 2025, reflecting the rapid expansion of bilateral economic engagement. Total trade in goods and services between the two countries reached £2.2bn in the four quarters to the end of the third quarter of 2025, according to UK government data.
He pointed to Uzbekistan’s sustained economic growth and reform programme as factors creating opportunities for British businesses, while highlighting the complementarity between the two countries’ economic priorities.
During the visit, Lord Sarwar also met President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, describing the meeting as positive and expressing gratitude for the president’s time.
Services lead bilateral trade opportunities
According to Lord Sarwar, Uzbekistan offers British businesses a combination of market size, economic growth and regional connectivity. With a population of more than 38mn and foreign trade turnover approaching $50bn in January–July 2026, the country is seeking to attract investment and strengthen its participation in international supply chains.
Services already account for approximately 80% of UK exports to Uzbekistan, reflecting Britain’s strengths in financial and professional business services.
He also highlighted opportunities in mining technology and consultancy, healthcare, education, aerospace and aviation, arguing that British companies could contribute more than products and investment.
For British companies considering entry into the Uzbek market, the minister emphasised the importance of building local relationships and maintaining a long-term commitment.
The British Embassy in Tashkent has a dedicated trade team that advises exporters, facilitates introductions to government and business contacts, and helps companies navigate the local commercial environment. Where appropriate, businesses can also explore financing options through UK Export Finance.
However, he stressed that institutional support alone would not guarantee success. British firms should take the time to understand the market, meet prospective partners and establish direct relationships with local businesses.
WTO accession and access to international markets
The UK supports Uzbekistan’s accession to the World Trade Organization (WTO), viewing membership as an important step towards deeper integration into the global trading system and greater confidence among international investors.
Lord Sarwar noted that the UK continued to encourage the economic reforms associated with accession, which could strengthen transparency, competition and predictability for businesses operating in the country.
WTO membership could also support Uzbekistan’s efforts to diversify exports and participate more fully in international supply chains.
Alongside supporting Uzbekistan’s accession, Britain is seeking to expand access to its own market for Uzbek exporters. Under the UK’s Developing Countries Trading Scheme, eligible goods from developing countries can enter Britain at reduced tariff rates.
Lord Sarwar encouraged Uzbek businesses to make greater use of the scheme as they seek to diversify exports and establish a stronger presence in the UK market. He also highlighted the role of the Uzbek Embassy in London in connecting exporters with British businesses and potential partners.
However, he cautioned that favourable tariff arrangements alone would not guarantee commercial success.
Closer cooperation between trade institutions, business associations and private companies could help Uzbek exporters obtain the necessary guidance, identify suitable partners and position their products more effectively in Britain.
London seeks a bigger role in Uzbekistan’s investment drive
International finance will be important to Uzbekistan’s economic transformation, according to Lord Sarwar, who highlighted London’s financial markets as a potential source of capital and specialist expertise.
The UK capital offers access to banks, asset managers, insurers, legal advisers and accountancy firms that can help Uzbek companies structure investment proposals, raise equity or debt and establish relationships with international investors.
Lord Sarwar pointed to the National Investment Fund of Uzbekistan (UzNIF), which has accessed the London Stock Exchange, as an example of progress in connecting the country’s assets with international capital markets.
However, he said attracting sustained investment would depend on Uzbekistan’s ability to maintain a transparent and predictable business environment.
Lord Sarwar expressed hope that more Uzbek companies would raise financing through the London Stock Exchange and that one or two major projects in Uzbekistan’s infrastructure modernisation programme would receive support from UK Export Finance.
Clean energy and critical minerals
Renewable energy is another potential area for cooperation, particularly as Uzbekistan seeks to diversify its energy mix and meet its climate objectives.
He also highlighted the role of finance in turning Uzbekistan’s renewable-energy ambitions into viable projects.
Closer cooperation between governments, financial institutions and private companies could combine Uzbekistan’s renewable-energy potential with British expertise in project development and sustainable finance, supporting energy security and economic diversification.
In the mining sector, Lord Sarwar identified three main areas for collaboration: technology, specialist services and investment.
British companies can provide advanced mining technologies and engineering solutions to improve productivity, operational efficiency and the responsible use of natural resources. He cited Weir Minerals as an example of British technology contributing to the modernisation of Uzbekistan’s mining industry.
The UK also has expertise in mining consultancy and professional services, which could help companies plan complex projects, use technology more efficiently and apply robust technical, commercial and environmental standards.
London’s capital markets could provide additional financing through initial public offerings, debt issuances and other financial instruments, connecting Uzbek companies with international investors.
He added that combining investment with technical expertise could help Uzbekistan develop more resilient supply chains and capture greater value from its mineral resources.
Fintech and digital innovation
The two countries also have opportunities to deepen cooperation in digital trade and technology, particularly where British expertise complements Uzbekistan’s growing pool of young talent and expanding digital economy.
He highlighted fintech as a particularly promising area, noting that Uzbek companies had already engaged with British counterparts on digital banking, tokenization and compliance technologies.
Further cooperation could extend to artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, digital construction and IT-enabled professional services.
The minister also called for stronger connections between businesses, universities, investors and innovation institutions to help Uzbek companies access international expertise and financing.
From growing trade to long-term partnerships
Looking ahead, Lord Sarwar said he wanted the UK–Uzbekistan economic relationship to become more diversified, with stronger trade flows, deeper investment ties and practical projects delivering benefits for both countries.
He also expressed hope that Uzbekistan would join the World Trade Organization and that more Uzbek companies would access international financing through the London Stock Exchange. Another priority would be securing support from UK Export Finance for major infrastructure modernisation projects in Uzbekistan.
However, Lord Sarwar stressed that the partnership’s success should not be measured by trade and investment figures alone.

high_priority_articles.title: The human cost of South Korea's AI chip boom - NST Online
high_priority_articles.summary: The human cost of South Korea's AI chip boom  NST Online
high_priority_articles.full_text:
SOUTH Korean activists campaigning for workplace safety in the nation's booming semiconductor industry are calling on the government to recognise the cancer diagnoses of three former SK Hynix employees as work-related illnesses.
SK Hynix, along with fellow South Korean tech giant Samsung Electronics, has emerged as a key player in the booming artificial intelligence industry, with its cutting-edge memory chips crucial to powering the sector's rapid growth.
Establishing direct links between semiconductor work and certain cancers can be contentious, with research inconclusive.
But fabrication and assembly plant workers can face exposure to solvents, acids, toxic metals and chemical gases, according to the United States Occupational Safety and Health Administration.
Samsung issued a public apology in 2018 to workers, many of them young women, who had developed cancer after working at some of its factories, paying out 150 million won per case after a decade-long dispute.
Supporters for the Health and Rights of People in the Semiconductor Industry (SHARPS), one of the groups that had pressured Samsung, said chemicals classified as carcinogens were being used by SK Hynix.
"We have confirmed that several substances on SK Hynix's own list of prohibited chemicals are in fact being used, including nickel and its compounds," Lee Sang-soo, a SHARPS activist, told a news conference, citing data reported by SK Hynix to the Environment Ministry.
SK Hynix said it was "taking various measures to more objectively identify the characteristics of disease occurrence" and was fully cooperating with government inquiries.
The company, which did not address the specific claims, said it had taken "proactive industrial health measures, including the development of a comprehensive support and compensation plan".
—AFP

high_priority_articles.title: SK Hynix Tests Memory Chips in Orbit Aboard South Korean Satellite - www.briefasia.com
high_priority_articles.summary: SK Hynix Tests Memory Chips in Orbit Aboard South Korean Satellite  www.briefasia.com
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Korea's Memory Giant Enters Space Testing
SK Hynix has deployed dynamic random-access memory and Universal Flash Storage products into orbit aboard a South Korean satellite, the company confirmed following the successful fifth launch of the country's Nuri rocket. The satellite established ground communication after reaching orbit, enabling what SK Hynix describes as in-orbit reliability testing for its memory components.
The deployment represents the Icheon-based chipmaker's first publicly disclosed venture into space-grade electronics, a niche but growing segment where radiation tolerance, extreme temperature resilience, and long-term reliability requirements differ sharply from consumer and enterprise applications.
Why Space Electronics Matter for Chipmakers
Space represents a technically demanding but strategically valuable market for semiconductor manufacturers. Satellites, deep-space probes, and orbital infrastructure require memory chips capable of withstanding cosmic radiation, temperature swings exceeding 150 degrees Celsius, and years of operation without repair or replacement.
Traditional space-qualified components undergo extensive ground-based testing and certification, processes that can stretch development cycles to five years or more. In-orbit validation accelerates this timeline, allowing manufacturers to assess real-world performance under conditions impossible to fully replicate in terrestrial laboratories.
For SK Hynix, the move signals interest in diversifying beyond its core smartphone, PC, and data centre markets. The global space economy reached USD 469 billion in 2025, according to the Space Foundation, with satellite constellations for broadband, Earth observation, and navigation driving demand for more capable onboard computing.
The Technical Challenge
DRAM and flash storage face distinct challenges in orbit. DRAM's volatile nature makes it vulnerable to single-event upsets, where a high-energy particle flips a bit in memory, potentially corrupting data or crashing systems. Flash storage, while non-volatile, suffers cumulative damage from radiation exposure that can degrade write endurance and data retention over time.
Aerospace engineers typically mitigate these risks through radiation-hardened designs, error-correction codes, and redundant architectures. Commercial off-the-shelf components, even from leading manufacturers, require validation to determine whether their inherent resilience meets mission requirements or whether additional shielding and fault tolerance are necessary.
SK Hynix has not disclosed which specific DRAM or UFS product lines flew aboard the satellite, nor whether the chips incorporate design modifications for space use. The company also has not announced a timeline for releasing test data or performance metrics from the orbital deployment.
Asia's Expanding Role in Space Infrastructure
South Korea's Nuri programme, managed by the Korea Aerospace Research Institute, achieved its first successful payload delivery to orbit in 2022 after two decades of development. The rocket can carry 1,500 kilograms to low Earth orbit, positioning South Korea as the seventh nation with indigenous orbital launch capability.
The programme's fifth launch continues a cadence aimed at establishing reliable, domestically controlled access to space, reducing reliance on foreign launch providers. For Korean technology companies, this opens opportunities to test and deploy hardware in orbit without navigating export controls or competing for limited slots on international missions.
Japan, China, and India have similarly expanded their space programmes in recent years, with commercial and government satellites increasingly carrying domestically produced electronics. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and Samsung Electronics have both explored radiation-tolerant process nodes, though neither has publicly committed to space-specific product lines.
What Comes Next
SK Hynix's orbital test represents an early-stage exploration rather than a commercial product announcement. The company has not indicated whether it plans to develop a dedicated space-grade memory portfolio, pursue partnerships with satellite manufacturers, or simply assess whether existing products can serve lower-risk orbital applications.
Results from the in-orbit testing will determine the next steps. If SK Hynix's standard DRAM and UFS products demonstrate acceptable error rates and longevity in space, the company could position itself as a supplier for the emerging class of commercial satellites that prioritise cost and performance over the ultra-high reliability demanded by scientific missions or crewed spacecraft.
The space electronics market remains a fraction of SK Hynix's revenue, but the strategic calculus extends beyond immediate sales. Demonstrating that memory chips can function in one of the most hostile environments known builds credibility for terrestrial applications in automotive, industrial, and defence sectors where reliability under stress is paramount.
For now, the chips are in orbit, the data are being collected, and the Korean memory industry has opened a new frontier.

high_priority_articles.title: Türkiye slams latest Houthi attack on Saudi capital Riyadh
high_priority_articles.summary: Türkiye on Sunday condemned "in the strongest terms" the latest Houthi attack targeting King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh, according to the Foreign...
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Türkiye on Sunday condemned "in the strongest terms" the latest Houthi attack targeting King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh, according to the Foreign Ministry.
"We condemn in the strongest terms the Houthi targeting of King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the capital of Saudi Arabia, once again," the ministry said in a statement.
Ankara expressed condolences to the families of those killed in the attack and wished a speedy recovery to the injured, while conveying its sympathies to the Saudi people.
"We wish Allah’s mercy upon those who lost their lives in the attacks and a speedy recovery to the injured," it added.
The ministry said attacks deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure and innocent civilians constitute clear violations of international law and the principles of international humanitarian law.
"These attacks, which target civilians and civilian infrastructure and further escalate tensions in the region, must cease immediately."
It also slammed actions that threaten regional security and stability while undermining the international community's joint efforts to establish peace.
"We reaffirm our full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and reiterate our call for the resolution of ongoing conflicts through dialogue and diplomacy," it added.

high_priority_articles.title: Iran war threatens Healey's Budget plans, think tank warns - BBC
high_priority_articles.summary: Iran war threatens Healey's Budget plans, think tank warns  BBC'Tax rises needed to plug £35bn gap' and 'Putin breaks Trump's 'ceasefire"  BBCUK's Healey can't risk a 'steady as you go' budget, think tank warns  ReutersIFS: budget will be ‘work of fiction’ without clear plan to cover UK spending pressures  The GuardianHealey Needs £35 Billion to Meet UK Spending Plans, IFS Says  Bloomberg.com
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The price spike caused by the US-Israel war in Iran poses a major challenge for Chancellor John Healey as he puts together his first Budget, an influential think tank has warned.
Higher-than-expected inflation could eat into what the government hoped to spend on public services, meaning Healey will have to choose between spending cuts, tax rises, or a mixture of both, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said.
It urged the government to ensure its spending plans are credible, as opposed to proposing unrealistic future cuts to make the Budget add up.
The Treasury declined to comment on "rumour and speculation".
However, speaking ahead of the annual International Monetary Fund meeting this week, Healey said: "The consequences of conflict in the Middle East and Europe are hitting countries worldwide, leading to higher prices at the pumps and more expensive mortgages at home.
"But Britain and our allies can face up to these challenges together."
He said his Budget "will build on this approach with fiscal discipline helping to deliver economic resilience" and give people "breathing space".
However, the government is under growing pressure to show financial markets that it has a tight grip on finances as the cost of borrowing rises.
The IFS cautioned Healey about making any spending announcements in the 28 October Budget speech he has no intention of honouring.
"A 'steady-as-she-goes' Budget is not an option available to the chancellor," said IFS director Helen Miller said.
"Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments' spending plans off course.
"Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the Budget a work of fiction," she added.
The US-Israel war against Iran and Russia's invasion of Ukraine have together helped drive up energy prices around the world.
These higher costs have been passed to customers via higher prices on shelves and at the pumps.
The wars have also contributed to a rise in the cost of UK government debt interest payments, adding to the pressure on Healey.
Although higher inflation will boost tax revenues, it will also eat into the value of departments' cash budgets, the IFS said.
'Breathing space'
Like other analysts, the IFS thinks recent turbulence on bond markets and higher inflation will add around £10bn to forecasts for the government's borrowing costs in 2029-30.
However, it still expects the government to meet its self-imposed fiscal rules - that it will only borrow for investment projects by the financial year 2029-30 and also be reducing debt as a percentage of GDP - not least as inflation pushes up tax revenues.
But it expects those rules to be met by a smaller buffer - known as "headroom" - of around £20bn. That is less than the £24bn buffer predicted at the time of the Spring Statement by the official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).
Recent indications have been that the markets would be comfortable with that degree of reduced headroom. The IFS also expects any "breathing space" help for households to be temporary and limited in scale.
However, the IFS warns that in such a volatile environment, its forecasts are exceptionally uncertain. And the official forecast from the OBR - which the chancellor relies on when making his plans - may come to a very different conclusion.
The IFS reckons that to maintain departments' budgets in the face of higher inflation, the government may need to find an extra £25bn in 2029-30.
That is before consider considering the ambition to raise defence spending. Raising such an amount would point to significant tax rises.
The chancellor does not have to address spending totals in this Budget, and may choose to leave such decisions until future events - for example, next year's Spring Statement or Spending Review - by which time the outlook for the economy could look very different.
But the IFS warned that the spending plans inherited from the previous chancellor, Rachel Reeves, would mean some departments' budgets would not keep pace with inflation in a few years time.
It said not addressing this would cast doubt on the credibility of the government's plans.
However, previous chancellors have relied on a similar strategy of pencilling in unrealistic future spending plans to ensure that they meet the fiscal rules on the day - only to change the plans further down the line.

high_priority_articles.title: Ethiopia, Eritrea ramp up rhetoric: Are they inching towards war? - Al Jazeera
high_priority_articles.summary: Ethiopia, Eritrea ramp up rhetoric: Are they inching towards war?  Al JazeeraEthiopia says it must defend itself against Eritrea's 'all-out invasion'  ReutersEthiopia and Eritrea are on the brink of another conflict  The EconomistEthiopia tells UN it is acting in self-defense against Eritrea  AP NewsEthiopia warns Eritrea it will defend itself after troops enter Tigray  BBC
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Ethiopia and Eritrea have exchanged accusations of aggression at the United Nations, raising fears of a new conflict in the Horn of Africa region as fighting intensifies in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region.
The diplomatic spat comes as Ethiopian troops and allied armed groups advanced across Tigray, where forces from Asmara have allegedly crossed the border to support rebels fighting the government forces.
Recommended Stories
The two neighbours, which fought a deadly border war between 1998 and 2000, were allies during Ethiopia’s devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war.
However, they have since been at loggerheads over the 2022 peace agreement that ended a two-year civil war between the government in Addis Ababa and Tigray rebels, and over Ethiopia’s demands for access to the Red Sea.
So, what did Eritrea and Ethiopia accuse each other of, and are they inching towards war?
What did Eritrea and Ethiopia say at the UN?
Eritrean troops had advanced as far as 60km (37 miles) into Tigray, Ethiopia told the UN Security Council on Friday, accusing its neighbour of violating its sovereignty.
In a letter, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos described the alleged incursion as “a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence”.
He invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter, which recognises a country’s right to self-defence, but did not specify what measures Ethiopia was taking.
Eritrea, which won independence from Ethiopia in 1993, rejected the accusations of incursions into Ethiopia, calling them a pretext for an Addis Ababa offensive.
Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh, in his own letter to the UN Security Council on Saturday, urged the body to condemn Ethiopia’s “deplorable declaration of war” and take “deterrent measures”.
He warned that an Ethiopian offensive would cause “huge devastation to the peoples of both countries and destabilise the whole region”.
The accusations come amid a broader dispute over access to the Red Sea.
Landlocked Ethiopia has repeatedly argued that securing direct sea access is essential, while Eritrea fears Addis Ababa intends to seize its port of Assab.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed reiterated on Monday that Ethiopia must have access to the Red Sea.
Hossamaldeen Ibrahim, an analyst at Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute (BISI), said the narratives of both countries contain “verifiable elements”.
“The danger lies in the fact that each side now treats the other’s narrative as existential,” he told Al Jazeera.
Eritrea and Ethiopia fought a deadly border war from 1998 to 2000. Relations improved after Abiy came to power in 2018, but have soured again in recent years.
Professor Matthias Rompel from the Institute of Sociology at the Justus-Liebig-University Giessen in Germany, said that both sides have legitimate security concerns, but their accusations need to be distinguished from independently verified facts.
“Ethiopia’s allegations of Eritrean military incursions into Tigray… and …the scale of Eritrean involvement, and particularly allegations that Asmara is orchestrating the rebellion against Addis Ababa, remain difficult to substantiate independently,” he told Al Jazeera.
He added that the latest developments suggest that the confrontation is no longer merely about Tigray. “Ethiopia’s quest for Red Sea access, Eritrea’s concerns about sovereignty, and Egypt’s strategic rivalry with Ethiopia over the Nile are interconnected,” he said.
“The conflict, therefore, has the potential to destabilise the wider Horn of Africa, with repercussions for Sudan, Somalia and Red Sea security.”
What is the latest fighting about, and how is Eritrea allegedly involved?
Fighting escalated on September 23 when a rebel alliance, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), launched attacks against Ethiopian government forces across Tigray, Amhara and Afar regions.
The rebels captured Tigray’s capital, Mekelle, and its airport before announcing their withdrawal on October 3. Government-allied forces subsequently entered the city.
In the latest on the battlefront, government and allied forces took Idaga Hamus early Friday and Abiy-Adi, in the Tembien area, on Thursday afternoon, according to Ermiyas Ababu, a commander of the government-allied Tigray Peace Force.
Residents, according to Reuters news agency, also reported the takeover of Idaga Hamus. Gebremedhin Kihishen, a business owner in Tembien, said government-allied forces controlled Abiy-Adi.
It was unclear from those accounts who held the towns immediately before the reported government advance or whether Eritrean troops were involved in the fighting.
Ermiyas previously reported Eritrean personnel entering Adigrat on Tuesday and Idaga Hamus on Wednesday, citing reports from his personnel. Al Jazeera was unable to independently verify the claims.
The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), a United States-based conflict monitor, reported that Eritrean troops crossed into Ethiopia near Zalambessa and came under Ethiopian drone attack while advancing towards Idaga Hamus. Eritrea has yet to comment on the development.
Addis Ababa accuses Asmara of financing, arming and directing armed groups, as well as deploying troops inside Tigray. Eritrea denies the allegations, which have not been independently verified.
The renewed fighting threatens to unravel the 2022 peace agreement.
That conflict began in November 2020 after months of tensions between Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and the TPLF, which had dominated Ethiopian politics for nearly three decades before Abiy took office in 2018.
Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF, its longtime adversary. The war killed hundreds of thousands of people and was marked by allegations of massacres, sexual violence and widespread hunger.
The November 2022 Pretoria agreement ended major hostilities, but Eritrea was not a party to the deal. Relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara subsequently deteriorated.
Has Ethiopia sent troops north towards Eritrea?
Multiple media reports say Ethiopian government troops and allied militias entered Adigrat, a strategic city roughly 30km (19 miles) from the Eritrean border, on Saturday.
Three residents confirmed their presence to Reuters, while verified footage showed government-allied militia members walking through the city.
Associated Press news agency footage also showed Ethiopian military vehicles entering Adigrat as some residents welcomed the troops.
Government-allied forces have reported capturing Idaga Hamus and Abiy-Adi, while explosions and alleged drone strikes have been reported near Adigrat.
Are Ethiopia and Eritrea inching towards war?
Analysts warn that Ethiopia and Eritrea may already have moved beyond threats and into a dangerous phase of possible military confrontation.
BISI’s Ibrahim said the two countries have moved beyond “inching” towards war, noting that “The situation has entered a high-risk phase of limited but direct military confrontation with a real possibility of rapid escalation into interstate war.”
He warned that the severing of diplomatic ties removed the “last formal mechanism for crisis management”, while Ethiopian military advances towards the Eritrean border increased the risk of “miscalculation”.
Tom Gardner, a correspondent for The Economist, said the current tensions should be understood in the context of decades of hostility between the neighbours.
Their brief alliance during the 2020-2022 Tigray war was an exception and was driven by a shared hostility towards the TPLF, Gardner told Al Jazeera.
“The Ethiopian government’s strategic goal number one is access to the Red Sea, but also removing Eritrea’s government from the picture,” he noted.
“It’s very much looking like the most dangerous moment for the region since that 1998 to 2000 war.”
Rompel from Justus-Liebig-University Giessen said that the current situation is evolving. “The danger of a wider interstate conflict is real, and the situation has already moved beyond a purely diplomatic confrontation,” he said.
“The central danger is not necessarily that either government has decided to launch a full-scale war, but that military miscalculations, mutual distrust and domestic political pressures could trigger a further escalation neither side can easily control.
“A wider conflict is not inevitable, but the space for diplomatic de-escalation is rapidly narrowing,” he said.
